facts.typicalSaleDate: Usually mid July through late August.
facts.registration: Yes. Buyers must register with the county clerk by the advertised deadline.
facts.redemptionPeriod: No short fixed deed redemption period. Owner can pay until the lien is enforced or foreclosed.

extra.label: Location or auction site
extra.value: Start with Bourbon County Clerk, 301 Main Street, Suite 106, Paris. Sale room is announced by the clerk.

extra.label: Registration Window
extra.value: State registration can open in October. County deadline is set in the annual local notice.

extra.label: Deposit or fees
extra.value: 100% deposit on priority claims. 25% deposit on current year nonpriority list. Fees capped yearly at $250.

Bourbon County sits in the heart of Kentucky horse country, with Paris as its county seat. For tax sale investors, this county follows Kentucky’s certificate of delinquency system, which is a tax lien certificate model rather than a true tax deed sale. This guide breaks down how Bourbon County tax sales work, where to check updates, what the auction process looks like, and what investors should know before spending money.

What is a brief overview of Bourbon County’s tax lien investing

Bourbon County sells certificates of delinquency on unpaid real property taxes through the county clerk. In Kentucky, unpaid bills move from the sheriff to the county clerk after April 15. Counties then hold tax sales no earlier than July 14, and most sales happen from mid July through late August. Investors are buying a tax lien claim with interest, not instant ownership of the real estate.

Important Details

Key Takeaways

  • Bourbon County follows a tax lien certificate system for unpaid property taxes, allowing investors to buy certificates of delinquency.
  • Tax sales occur from mid July to late August, and buyers must register with the county clerk by the deadline.
  • Investors can expect a 12% simple interest rate, with opportunities for both local and foreign investors to participate.
  • Due diligence is crucial; investors should carefully research properties, as liens may be tied to vacant lots or low-value land.
  • Buying unsold certificates after tax sales offers a chance for less competition and longer review times.

Fun Facts About the County

  • Bourbon County is one of Kentucky’s oldest counties and Paris is the county seat.
  • The county had about 20,243 people and 9,289 housing units in recent Census data.
  • More than 50 horse farms are in the county, including Claiborne Farm.
  • Colville Covered Bridge, built in 1877, is one of only 13 covered bridges left in Kentucky.

Attractions & Economic Highlights

  • Attractions: Claiborne Farm, Colville Covered Bridge, Duncan Tavern, Secretariat Park.
  • Transportation: Bourbon County is in Kentucky Highway District 7. Major routes include US 27, US 68, and US 460. Blue Grass Airport serves the larger area.
  • Economy: Horse farms, agriculture, and manufacturing all matter here.
  • Community: Outdoor drives, farm visits, creek and bridge stops, and downtown Paris events help local appeal.

Why This County is Ideal for Tax Lien Investors

  • Kentucky tax lien certificates can offer high returns because the statutory rate is 12% simple interest.
  • Bourbon County has a steady housing base and a median owner occupied home value above $229,000 in recent Census data.
  • This is a low risk investment only when the lien amount is small compared with real property value and title issues are checked first.
  • The county gives investors access to state tax lien opportunities in a well known central Kentucky market with horse, farm, and town property types.

Auction Process for Tax Lien Sales

Bourbon County follows Kentucky’s county clerk tax sale rules. That means the sale is not a bid down interest auction. The interest rate is set by law at 12%. Instead, buyers register, submit required lists, and the clerk allocates certificates using priority rights and a random drawing order. The price starts at the amount due, plus allowed fees and costs.

How the Auction Works

Here is a simple look at how the Bourbon County tax lien sale works from notice through post-sale rights.

  1. Register before the deadline

    File the county form, any state registration proof that applies, your certificate lists, fees, and deposits.

  2. Report to the clerk

    Registered buyers report to the county clerk’s office on sale day for instructions and the final sale list.

  3. Priority claims go first

    If you already hold a prior year lien on the same property, you may get first claim to the current year certificate.

  4. Random order controls rounds

    After priority claims, the clerk uses a random drawing to set the order for each round of selection.

  5. Pay the balance

    Deposits are applied to what you buy. Any extra amount due is paid as the clerk directs. Refunds on unused deposit money are due after the sale.

Maximum Potential Returns and Expected Returns on Bourbon County Tax Lien Certificates

The headline return is 12% simple interest per year. That is the legal rate attached to the certificate. Your actual yield depends on how fast the owner pays, what added costs are allowed, and whether you later spend money on notice work or court action. If the lien is paid soon, your dollar profit may be modest even though the rate is good. If it stays unpaid longer, the return can grow, but so can your risk and legal cost. In Bourbon County, the best results often come from smaller liens attached to real property with solid value and clear title history.

Open to All Investors /Foreign Investor Participation

Kentucky’s system is built around third party purchasers, and the official state guidance explains how outside buyers register and take part. The public sources reviewed did not show a Bourbon County rule that limits the sale to local residents only. That means out of state investors can usually take part if they meet the registration, fee, and deposit rules.

For foreign investors, the main issue is not nationality. The real issue is process. You need a way to submit forms, handle funds accepted by the clerk, receive notices, and manage follow up collection work in the United States. Before joining, ask the clerk what payment methods are accepted and whether any local filing step needs an in person visit.

Importance of Due Diligence in Bourbon County Tax Lien Investing

Buying a lien is not the same as buying a safe asset. You still need to study the property, its use, and its value. In Bourbon County, the online delinquent list includes many vacant lots, mobile home entries, and lower balance bills. That means you should check whether the lien is tied to land, an improvement, or a mobile home setup before you bid.

What Due Diligence Entails

  • Check the parcel and property type.
  • Review map ID, owner name, and address match.
  • Study market value and resale demand.
  • Check access, occupancy, and land use.
  • Review title issues and later court cost risk.

Risks of Skipping Due Diligence

  • You may buy on low value land.
  • Mobile home or odd parcel issues can hurt resale.
  • Extra legal work can cut returns.
  • A long hold can tie up cash.
  • Bad records can make enforcement harder.

Buying Over the Counter liens in Bourbon County

How to Purchase OTC Liens

Yes. Kentucky allows any remaining certificates to be bought after the tax sale. State guidance says that once the county sale is complete, unsold certificates may be purchased at any time by any qualified third party purchaser, subject to ongoing registration rules and per certificate fees. That is the closest thing to an OTC market in Bourbon County.

Benefits of OTC Purchases

OTC buying can be easier because there is no sale day rush. You get more time to review each certificate and may avoid round by round competition. The interest rate is still set by law.

Why Bourbon County is a Top Choice for Tax Lien Investors

Economic and Tax Advantages

  • Central Kentucky location near Lexington helps market access.
  • Horse farms, agriculture, and manufacturing support the local economy.
  • Kentucky lien certificates carry 12% simple interest by statute.

Real Estate Market Overview

Bourbon County has a mix of town lots, rural tracts, farm related land, and some mobile home related tax bills. Recent Census data shows a median owner occupied home value of $229,300 and median gross rent of $822. That mix can give investors choices, but it also means each parcel needs its own review before purchase.

Conclusion

Bourbon County is a Kentucky tax lien certificate county. The county clerk handles the sale, the sheriff transfers unpaid bills after April 15, and the sale season usually falls between mid July and late August. The legal interest rate is 12% simple interest, and unsold certificates may still be available after the live sale.

That said, smart investing here starts with careful research. Check the clerk site, the state tax sale rules, and the parcel details before you spend money. In Bourbon County, a small lien on a clean parcel can be far better than a cheap lien on a problem property. Good research is what turns a tax lien idea into a smart investing decision.

Pro Tips

  • Focus first on real estate parcels, not mobile home entries, unless you know that niche well.
  • Paris area lots may be easier to value than remote tracts because market comps are easier to find.
  • Keep a short list ready before sale day so the random round system does not slow you down.
  • Ask the clerk what payment forms are accepted before sale day. Do not guess.
  • Track nearby counties too. Kentucky sales run in a tight summer window, so planning across counties helps.

FAQs for Bourbon County Tax Lien Certificates

Can I renovate right after buying the lien?

No. A lien certificate does not give you possession.

Do I get a deed at the sale?

No. You buy a lien claim, not the deed.

Will other liens disappear?

Not just because you bought the certificate. Later enforcement steps matter.

Can I finance the purchase later?

You should expect to fund deposits and balances yourself unless the clerk allows otherwise.

Do I need quiet title right away?

Not at the lien stage. That issue comes later if the case becomes a deed matter.
